name: Rigetti Financial Struggles
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Cash, Splits, and Survival: Rigetti's Bumpy Road as a Public Company
lesson.summary: Rigetti Computing's path from SPAC debut to a Nasdaq-compliance reverse stock split illustrates, in concrete terms, what happens when a capital-intensive quantum hardware company's cash burn outpaces its ability to raise money on favorable terms.
lesson.body:
Rigetti Computing, a superconducting-qubit quantum computing company, went public in March 2022 through a SPAC merger with Supernova Partners Acquisition Company II, following the same general path that IonQ had taken a few months earlier and inheriting the same structural risks described in the previous chapter: sponsor dilution, redemption-driven cash shortfalls, and merger-era projections that would soon be tested against real quarterly results.

Like other early-stage quantum hardware companies, Rigetti has reported sustained annual net losses considerably larger than its revenue in the years since going public, a direct expression of the corporate R&D burn rate and revenue model problems examined earlier in this chapter. The company has continued funding chip fabrication, cryogenic infrastructure, and specialized R&D staff without a commensurate revenue base to offset that spending, which is precisely the dynamic that makes burn rate and runway such a decisive factor for companies at this stage regardless of how promising their underlying technical roadmap looks.

That financial pressure became visible in the company's share price and, eventually, in its capital structure. As Rigetti's stock fell well below Nasdaq's minimum bid price requirement of one dollar per share following its SPAC debut, the company executed a reverse stock split, consolidating a large number of existing shares into one new share to lift the nominal share price back above the compliance threshold; Rigetti carried out a reverse split on this order in 2023. This is a mechanical corporate action available to any public company facing a delisting risk, and it is not unique to quantum computing, but it is a clear, dated marker of financial distress in the company's public history.

It is worth being precise about why a reverse split is a warning sign rather than a fix. The split does not change the underlying value of the company, add any cash to its balance sheet, or improve its business fundamentals in any way; it is purely a mechanical rearrangement of how many shares represent the same total equity value, undertaken to satisfy a stock exchange's listing rule about minimum nominal price. It treats the symptom, a share price too low to remain listed, without touching the cause, which is the market's underlying valuation of the business given its continued losses and unresolved revenue model. A company that needs a reverse split is, definitionally, signaling that it has already lost most of its value relative to its public debut.

Rigetti's experience functions as a concrete case study where nearly every concept in this chapter converges on one company: it was born from the VC funding frenzy of 2021, it chose the SPAC route with the structural risks that entails, it has burned cash at a rate typical of quantum hardware R&D, and it has struggled to build the kind of recurring, disclosed revenue relationship that would let public markets value it on fundamentals rather than narrative about its technical roadmap. None of this proves Rigetti's underlying superconducting-qubit technology lacks merit; mature deep-tech fields have repeatedly seen early public companies struggle financially years before the eventual winning approach becomes clear. But the struggles are real, documented in public filings, and instructive precisely because they show, in concrete numbers rather than abstractions, what happens when hype-driven public valuation collides with the slower, harder reality of hardware R&D timelines.
